blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a study that examines bias in word embeddings and its propagation into downstream machine learning models. The paper demonstrates that word embeddings trained on corpora like Wikipedia or social media embed societal biases, which are then perpetuated in models using these embeddings. The authors show that bias can be measured (e.g., via cosine distance between gendered word pairs) and is particularly insidious because embeddings strip words of their original context, freezing bias into static representations. The study also explores mitigation strategies, finding that debiasing at the classifier level is more effective than at the embedding level, as the latter may leave uncorrected biases intact. Additionally, the paper shows that biased embeddings can be repurposed to detect bias in new text samples, achieving high accuracy in classifying sexist comments when trained on similarly biased embeddings.
paper_abstract: Social bias in language — towards genders, ethnicities, ages, and other social groups — poses a problem with ethical impact for many NLP applications. Recent research has shown that machine learning models trained on respective data may not only adopt, but even amplify the bias. So far, however, little attention has been paid to bias in computational argumentation. In this paper, we study the existence of social biases in large English debate portals. In particular, we train word embedding models on portal-specific corpora and systematically evaluate their bias using W EAT, an existing metric to measure bias in word embeddings. In a word co-occurrence analysis, we then investigate causes of bias. The results suggest that all tested debate corpora contain unbalanced and biased data, mostly in favor of male people with European-American names. Our empirical insights contribute towards an understanding of bias in argumentative data sources.
